messages.subject: posterior mean of latent random field
parts:
Hi All,

In SPDE tutorial, I have a problem with posterior mean of latent random field. For example in toy model example:

Let X denote the latent random field.

In INLA, chapter 3, the poterior mean of latent random field obtained is: res5$summary.random$i$mean

But in SPDE theory, I got formulas from Finn's papers, I have

X~N(mu, Qx)
Y|X=x ~ N(A x, Qeps)

The posterior distribution for X given Y=y is then given by

X|Y=y ~ N(mupost, Qpost)

Where

Qpost = Qx + A' Qeps A
mupost = mu + Qpost^-1 A' Qeps (y - A mu)

I calculated manually mupost (posterior mean of X), and the result was much different from res5$summary.random$i$mean

Can you please explain me?

Thanks!

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] posterior mean of latent random field
parts:
There are a few problems here, mostly to do with the interpretation of the formulas.  

- The first big problem is that inla.qinv *does not* compute the inverse of Q!  (Q is a large sparse matrix - you never want to compute its actual inverse, that would be too computationally expensive).  For the record, inla.qinv(Q) computes enough elements of Q^{-1} to compute the Fisher score function (which turns out to be the elements of Q^{-1} correpsonding the non-zero elements of Q).  

- The second big problem is that in the formula for the posterior mean, mu is the prior mean and *not* a sample from the prior.  The correct code would be 
      mupost = mu + inla.qsolve(Qx+A5TQeps%*%A5, ASTQesp%*%(y- A5%*%mu)
where  mu is the mean of the prior (which is zero).  Note that inla.qsolve is the function (rather than inla.qinv) that you need here.

- The third problem, which is less big, is that even if this was computed correctly, it would not be the same as res5$summary.random$i$mean.  The thing calculated above is the mean of the latent field computed using the plug-in estimates of the hyperparamters (computed as their posterior expectation), whereas the result from the inla call is the mean of the marginal distribution computed by marginalising out the hyperparameters.  These are mathematically different quantities. 

I hope this helps.

D

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] posterior mean of latent random field
parts:
A basic rule in computation is that you almost never need to compute an actual matrix inverse.  With inla.qsolve(Q,b) we solve the linear system Qx=b, which is all that is needed in this situation.  It would be completely infeasible in most cases to compute the full inverse.  

So my main suggestion for computing the full inverse is to check if you really really need it.  (And really almost always you don't - you only need to solve a linear system or you need a few elements of the inverse [see q.inv])  

If you do, solve(as.matrix(Q)) will do the job, but it will be insanely expensive in terms of time and memory. In this case, I strongly suggest moving to an inference method that *doesn't* require the inverse of a large matrix.

For maximum likelihood estimates, you don't need the full inverse.

Best wishes,

Dan.

Hi Daniel,

Thank you for your explanation!

This is a beautiful suggestion if I intend to use the inverse of a large matrix.

Kind Regards,

On Thursday, November 28, 2013 1:44:13 PM UTC+11, Daniel Simpson wrote:

A basic rule in computation is that you almost never need to compute an actual matrix inverse.  With inla.qsolve(Q,b) we solve the linear system Qx=b, which is all that is needed in this situation.  It would be completely infeasible in most cases to compute the full inverse.  

So my main suggestion for computing the full inverse is to check if you really really need it.  (And really almost always you don't - you only need to solve a linear system or you need a few elements of the inverse [see q.inv])  

If you do, solve(as.matrix(Q)) will do the job, but it will be insanely expensive in terms of time and memory. In this case, I strongly suggest moving to an inference method that *doesn't* require the inverse of a large matrix.

For maximum likelihood estimates, you don't need the full inverse.

Best wishes,
Dan.
On 28 Nov 2013, at 03:38, Linh Nguyen <linh.vaw...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Daniel,

You are wonderful. Thank you so much for your help!
I got the correct results.

About inverse of Qpost: Do you have any suggestions to calcualte its acutual inverse? If we can't apply inla.qinv(), we have to find somehow to calculate its actual inverse like inla.qsolve() in this case, isn't it?

In section 2.5 in SPDE tutorial, page 24, the authors proposed a function to calculate invertible matrices by using Woodbury matrix identity, called precy.f. Inside this funcion, we utilized inla.qinv() too. Do you think this usage causes problems for maximum likelihood estimations?

Thanks!

On Wednesday, November 27, 2013 5:37:56 PM UTC+11, Daniel Simpson wrote:

There are a few problems here, mostly to do with the interpretation of the formulas.  

- The first big problem is that inla.qinv *does not* compute the inverse of Q!  (Q is a large sparse matrix - you never want to compute its actual inverse, that would be too computationally expensive).  For the record, inla.qinv(Q) computes enough elements of Q^{-1} to compute the Fisher score function (which turns out to be the elements of Q^{-1} correpsonding the non-zero elements of Q).  

- The second big problem is that in the formula for the posterior mean, mu is the prior mean and *not* a sample from the prior.  The correct code would be 
      mupost = mu + inla.qsolve(Qx+A5TQeps%*%A5, ASTQesp%*%(y- A5%*%mu)
where  mu is the mean of the prior (which is zero).  Note that inla.qsolve is the function (rather than inla.qinv) that you need here.

- The third problem, which is less big, is that even if this was computed correctly, it would not be the same as res5$summary.random$i$mean.  The thing calculated above is the mean of the latent field computed using the plug-in estimates of the hyperparamters (computed as their posterior expectation), whereas the result from the inla call is the mean of the marginal distribution computed by marginalising out the hyperparameters.  These are mathematically different quantities. 

I hope this helps.

D

On Wednesday, November 27, 2013 2:00:01 PM UTC+11, Daniel Simpson wrote:
This may be easier if you post your code. But were I to guess, I would say it's the hyper parameters. Finn's formulas are conditional on theta (the vector containing the noise precision and the range and precision parameters for the spde) whereas the inla mean output has integrated those parameters out.
